course.title: Mandarin Chinese: Foundations
course.description: An English-language introduction to Mandarin Chinese, also called Standard Chinese or Putonghua, for complete beginners: who speaks it, the four tones and the neutral tone, Pinyin romanization, how Chinese characters work, numbers, greetings, and simple sentences. The course is informed by the open encyclopedia article on Standard Chinese from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, which is released under CC BY-SA 4.0. Every Chinese example is paired with Pinyin and an English meaning, so you can start reading and saying real words from the very first lesson.

questions.prompt: What is another common name for Mandarin Chinese?
questions.explanation: Mandarin is the standardized national language, called Putonghua in mainland China - see 'What Mandarin is and who speaks it'.

questions.prompt: How many main tones does Mandarin have, not counting the neutral tone?
questions.explanation: Mandarin has four main tones, plus a fifth 'neutral' tone - see 'The sound system and the tones'.

options: a system that writes Mandarin sounds with the Latin alphabet
an ancient form of Chinese poetry
questions.explanation: Pinyin uses the familiar Latin letters, plus tone marks, to spell out how a word sounds - see 'Pinyin: reading the sounds'.
The Chinese characters are called Hanzi; Hiragana is Japanese, Hangul is Korean, and Cyrillic is used for Russian - see 'Chinese characters'.

questions.prompt: The greeting 你好 (nǐ hǎo) means...
questions.explanation: 你好 (nǐ hǎo) literally means 'you good' and is the standard way to say hello.

questions.prompt: Changing the tone of a Mandarin syllable...
options: can change the meaning of the word
questions.explanation: Tone is part of the word: mā, má, mǎ, and mà are four different words - see 'The sound system and the tones'.

questions.prompt: The basic word order of a simple Mandarin sentence is...
questions.explanation: Mandarin, like English, normally puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object - see 'Building simple sentences'.

questions.prompt: Which particle is added to the end of a statement to turn it into a yes/no question?
questions.explanation: Adding 吗 (ma) to a plain statement turns it into a yes/no question - see 'Building simple sentences'.

lessons.title: What Mandarin is and who speaks it
lessons.grammar_note: 'Chinese' names a whole branch of related languages; Mandarin is the largest one, and it is the standard taught around the world.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to say what Mandarin Chinese is, give its other common names, and name the main places where it is spoken as a first or official language. You will also be able to place Mandarin inside the larger family of Chinese languages and explain why it is often called the most widely spoken language in the world. Warm-up: before you read on, ask yourself whether 'Chinese' is a single language or a whole group of related languages. The answer turns out to be more interesting than a plain yes or no. Getting these big facts straight early is useful, because it tells you exactly what you are learning when you study Mandarin, and it keeps you from mixing Mandarin up with the other Chinese languages, such as Cantonese, that you may have heard of. With that map in hand, every later lesson on sounds, characters, and sentences will have a clear place to sit, and you will understand why this one variety is the one offered in classrooms almost everywhere.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Mandarin Chinese is the standardized national language of China, where it is called 普通话 (Pǔtōnghuà), meaning 'common speech'. In Taiwan the same standard is called 国语 (Guóyǔ), 'national language', and among Chinese communities in Singapore and Malaysia it is called 华语 (Huáyǔ). English speakers usually gather all of these under the single name Mandarin, or Standard Chinese. The standard pronunciation is based on the speech of Beijing in the north. Here is the key point: Chinese is not one language but a branch of the Sino-Tibetan family, and it holds several large groups that are not mutually intelligible when spoken, among them Mandarin, Cantonese (广东话, Guǎngdōnghuà), and others. Mandarin is by far the largest, with roughly a billion first-language speakers, which makes it the most spoken first language on earth. Yet although the spoken varieties sound very different, they share one writing system: the Chinese characters you will meet later can be read by educated speakers across these groups, even when they could not understand one another out loud.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Here are the core naming words, each with Pinyin and meaning. 中文 (Zhōngwén) is a general word for 'the Chinese language', especially the written language. 汉语 (Hànyǔ) means 'the Han language', another everyday word for Chinese. 普通话 (Pǔtōnghuà) is 'Mandarin / common speech'. 中国 (Zhōngguó) is 'China', literally 'middle country'. 中国人 (Zhōngguó rén) means 'a Chinese person'. Put them to work: 我说中文 (Wǒ shuō Zhōngwén) means 'I speak Chinese', where 我 (wǒ) is 'I', 说 (shuō) is 'speak', and 中文 (Zhōngwén) is 'Chinese'. 他是中国人 (Tā shì Zhōngguó rén) means 'He is a Chinese person', with 他 (tā) 'he', 是 (shì) 'is', and 中国人 (Zhōngguó rén) 'Chinese person'. Notice how the same small building blocks reappear: once you know 中 (zhōng, middle) and 人 (rén, person), you can already see them inside 中国 and 中国人. Collecting these high-frequency words now gives you a solid base for the lessons that follow.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each one, then check yourself. 1) What is the mainland Chinese name for the Mandarin standard? 2) Is Cantonese the same spoken language as Mandarin? 3) What writing system do the different Chinese languages share? 4) What does 中国 (Zhōngguó) mean, literally? 5) Roughly how many people speak Mandarin as a first language? 6) What does 中国人 (Zhōngguó rén) mean? Answers: 1) 普通话 (Pǔtōnghuà), 'common speech'. 2) No - Cantonese and Mandarin are separate spoken varieties that are not mutually intelligible by ear, though they share the written characters. 3) the Chinese characters (Hanzi). 4) 'middle country'. 5) roughly a billion people, making it the world's most spoken first language. 6) 'a Chinese person'. If you can answer these, you have the big map of the language firmly in place.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'Chinese' as a single spoken language - it is really a branch of related languages, and Mandarin is the largest standardized member. Mistake: assuming that because Cantonese and Mandarin share characters, speakers can understand each other out loud; the writing is shared, but the spoken forms are not mutually intelligible. Mistake: thinking the many names (Putonghua, Guoyu, Huayu) point to different languages; they are regional names for essentially the same standard. Exit ticket: (a) What single name do English speakers give the standard national language? (b) Name two different Chinese spoken varieties. (c) What do all of them have in common on the page? Answers: Mandarin, or Standard Chinese; Mandarin and Cantonese (others also count); they share the same system of Chinese characters.

lessons.title: The sound system and the tones
lessons.grammar_note: A Mandarin syllable is an initial plus a final plus a tone; change the tone and you change the word, so the tone is part of the spelling.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe how a Mandarin syllable is built, name and recognize the four main tones plus the neutral tone, and explain, with the famous 'ma' example, why tones change the meaning of a word. Warm-up: say the English word 'ma' three ways - flat, rising as in a question, and sharply falling as in a command. In Mandarin those pitch shapes are not emotion or emphasis; they are built into the word itself. This is often the single biggest surprise for English speakers, and getting comfortable with it early removes most of the fear people feel about Chinese. Tones are not a trap; they are simply one more feature of a word that you learn along with its sound and meaning, just as you learn whether an English word is stressed on its first or second syllable.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A Mandarin syllable has up to three parts: an initial consonant, a final (a vowel, sometimes with a closing sound), and a tone that sits over the whole syllable. The tone is the pitch shape of your voice. There are four main tones. The first tone is high and flat, written with a level mark, as in mā. The second tone rises from middle to high, as in má, like the pitch of an English question. The third tone dips down and then rises, as in mǎ. The fourth tone falls sharply from high to low, as in mà, like a firm command. There is also a fifth, neutral tone: short, light, and said with no particular pitch, written with no mark at all, as in the question word ma. Because the tone belongs to the word, two syllables that share the same letters but carry different tones are simply different words, as the next section shows plainly.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: The classic set uses the syllable 'ma' in all five tones, and each is a real word. 妈 (mā, first tone) means 'mother'. 麻 (má, second tone) means 'hemp' or 'numb'. 马 (mǎ, third tone) means 'horse'. 骂 (mà, fourth tone) means 'to scold'. And 吗 (ma, neutral tone) is the little question particle you add to the end of a sentence. So 妈骂马 (Mā mà mǎ) means 'Mother scolds the horse' - three different words that all look like 'ma' in plain letters but differ only in tone. A couple more pairs show the same lesson: 买 (mǎi) means 'to buy', while 卖 (mài) means 'to sell' - a dipping third tone versus a falling fourth tone flips buying into selling. Likewise 问 (wèn) is 'to ask' and 吻 (wěn) is 'to kiss'. Always learn a new word together with its tone, the way you would learn its spelling.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer or identify, then check. 1) Which tone is high and flat? 2) What does 马 (mǎ) mean, and which tone is it? 3) What does the neutral-tone word 吗 (ma) do in a sentence? 4) Which falls sharply, the second tone or the fourth tone? 5) 妈 (mā) and 骂 (mà) share the same letters - why are they different words? 6) What is the difference between 买 (mǎi) and 卖 (mài)? Answers: 1) the first tone, as in mā. 2) 'horse', and it is the third tone (the dipping tone). 3) it marks the sentence as a yes/no question. 4) the fourth tone falls sharply; the second tone rises. 5) because the tone is part of the word, so a first tone (mā, mother) and a fourth tone (mà, to scold) are not the same word. 6) 买 (mǎi, third tone) is 'to buy' and 卖 (mài, fourth tone) is 'to sell'.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating tones as mood or emphasis rather than as part of the word; saying 'horse' with a falling tone turns it into 'to scold'. Mistake: ignoring the neutral tone, which is light and short rather than stressed; forcing a full tone onto the question word ma makes it sound wrong. Mistake: confusing the third tone, which dips and then rises, with the fourth, which only falls. Practice the whole 'ma' set out loud until the five shapes feel distinct. Exit ticket: (a) How many main tones are there, and what is the extra one called? (b) What does 买 (mǎi) mean? (c) Why do 妈 (mā) and 马 (mǎ) count as different words? Answers: four main tones plus the neutral tone; 'to buy'; because they carry different tones, and the tone is part of the word.

lessons.title: Numbers one to nine and counting

items.example: 一个人 (yí gè rén - one person). Note: 一 is often said yí or yì before other words because of tone changes.
三本书 (sān běn shū - three books).
四个苹果 (sì gè píngguǒ - four apples).
八岁 (bā suì - eight years old). The number 八 is considered lucky.
九十九 (jiǔshíjiǔ - ninety-nine). For ten use 十 (shí), so eleven is 十一 (shíyī) and twenty is 二十 (èrshí).

lessons.title: Pinyin: reading the sounds
lessons.grammar_note: Pinyin spells each syllable as an initial plus a final, with a tone mark placed over the main vowel; a few letters do not sound the way English readers first expect.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to read a Pinyin syllable correctly, locate where the tone mark sits, and avoid the handful of letters that trick English readers. Warm-up: you already met Pinyin in the last two lessons, in words like Pǔtōnghuà and mā; now you will learn the system behind it. Pinyin, whose full name 拼音 (pīnyīn) means 'spell sound', is the official romanization that writes Mandarin with the Latin alphabet plus tone marks. It is how children on the mainland first learn to read, how you type Chinese on a keyboard, and how this whole course gives you the sound of every character. Mastering it is the fastest route into spoken Mandarin, because once you can read Pinyin aloud you can pronounce any new word the course shows you, long before you can recognize its character.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Each Pinyin syllable splits into an initial (the opening consonant, if any) and a final (the vowel part that follows). In mā the initial is m and the final is a; in shuō the initial is sh and the final is uo. Most consonants are close to English, but a few need care. The letter c sounds like the 'ts' in 'cats', so cài (dish) is roughly 'tsai'. The letter q sounds like a light 'ch', as in qī (seven), close to 'chee'. The letter x is a soft 'sh', as in xièxie (thank you). The letter z is like the 'ds' in 'reads'. Among the vowels, the letter combination that looks like 'ui' is really 'way', and 'iu' is 'yo'. The tone mark always goes over the main vowel of the final: in hǎo it sits over the a, in xué over the e. When you type, you leave the marks out and let the computer offer the characters.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Read these aloud, trusting the rules above. 你好 (nǐ hǎo) is 'hello'; the marks show third tone then third tone. 谢谢 (xièxie) is 'thank you'; the x is a soft 'sh', and the second syllable is neutral tone, so it is light. 中国 (Zhōngguó) is 'China'; zh is like the 'j' in 'jungle'. 老师 (lǎoshī) is 'teacher'; sh is like English 'sh'. 请 (qǐng) is 'please'; the q is that light 'ch'. 水 (shuǐ) is 'water'; the final ui sounds like 'way', so it is close to 'shway'. 六 (liù) is 'six'; the iu sounds like 'yo', so it is close to 'lyo'. Notice how the tone mark hunts for the strongest vowel: a first if there is one, then o or e, as in hǎo, Zhōngguó, and xué.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer or read, then check. 1) In the syllable 'shuō', what is the initial and what is the final? 2) How is the letter x pronounced, as in xièxie? 3) Over which vowel does the tone mark sit in hǎo? 4) How does the combination 'ui' in shuǐ really sound? 5) What does 拼音 (pīnyīn) mean? 6) How is the q in qī (seven) pronounced? Answers: 1) the initial is sh and the final is uo. 2) like a soft 'sh'. 3) over the a, giving hǎo. 4) like the English word 'way', so shuǐ is close to 'shway'. 5) 'spell sound'. 6) like a light 'ch', so qī sounds close to 'chee'. Reading Pinyin aloud a little every day quickly makes these rules automatic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading Pinyin letters with their plain English values; c is 'ts', q is a light 'ch', x is a soft 'sh', and zh is like 'j', not the sounds those letters usually carry in English. Mistake: putting the tone mark on the wrong vowel; it belongs over the main vowel of the final, as in hǎo and xué. Mistake: giving the neutral-tone second syllable of xièxie a full heavy tone instead of saying it lightly. Exit ticket: (a) What two parts make up every Pinyin syllable? (b) How is x pronounced? (c) Where does the tone mark go? Answers: an initial and a final; as a soft 'sh'; over the main vowel of the final.

lessons.title: Chinese characters: how Hanzi work
lessons.grammar_note: Each character is one syllable and one unit of meaning; many characters combine a meaning part (radical) with a sound part, and each is written with set strokes in a fixed order.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain what Chinese characters are, describe how radicals and sound parts combine inside many of them, tell simplified characters from traditional ones, and name the idea of stroke order. Warm-up: look at 林 (lín, forest) and 木 (mù, tree) - can you see one picture hiding inside the other? Characters reward this kind of looking. English spelling records sounds; Chinese characters, called 汉字 (Hànzì), mostly record whole words or units of meaning, which is why they can be read across spoken varieties that sound nothing alike. There are thousands of them, which sounds daunting, but they are built from a small set of repeating parts, so learning them is less like memorizing random shapes and more like learning to spot familiar pieces inside new combinations.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A Chinese character, 汉字 (Hànzì), is usually one syllable and one unit of meaning. The simplest are pictures grown abstract: 人 (rén) 'person', 木 (mù) 'tree', 水 (shuǐ) 'water', 山 (shān) 'mountain'. Characters combine: two trees make 林 (lín) 'woods', three make 森 (sēn) 'forest'. Most characters, though, pair a meaning part, the radical (部首, bùshǒu), with a sound part. In 妈 (mā, mother) the left side 女 (nǚ) is the 'woman' radical giving the meaning, and the right side 马 (mǎ) is there mostly for the sound. Radicals are how dictionaries are organized. Two written standards exist: simplified characters (简体字, jiǎntǐzì), used on the mainland and in Singapore, trim the stroke counts of many characters, while traditional characters (繁体字, fántǐzì), used in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau, keep the older fuller forms. So 'horse' is 马 simplified and 馬 traditional. Every character is drawn with a set number of strokes (笔画, bǐhuà) in a fixed order, generally top to bottom and left to right.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Build meaning from parts, each with Pinyin and sense. 木 (mù) 'tree', doubled to 林 (lín) 'woods', tripled to 森 (sēn) 'forest'. 水 (shuǐ) 'water' appears in a squeezed radical form on the left of many characters, so water-related words often carry it. The sound-plus-meaning pattern is everywhere: 妈 (mā, mother) is 女 (woman, meaning) plus 马 (mǎ, sound). The word for 'good', 好 (hǎo), joins 女 (nǚ, woman) and 子 (zǐ, child). The simplified-versus-traditional contrast shows clearly in common words: 'China' is 中国 simplified and 中國 traditional, and 'language' is 语 simplified and 語 traditional. For stroke order, 十 (shí, ten) is written as the horizontal stroke first, then the vertical: two strokes, drawn in that order. Learning a few radicals, such as 女, 木, 水, and 口 (kǒu, mouth), lets you guess at the meaning of many new characters.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check. 1) What does 汉字 (Hànzì) mean? 2) In 妈 (mā), which part gives the meaning and which gives the sound? 3) What does doubling 木 (mù) to make 林 (lín) mean? 4) Where are simplified characters mainly used, and where are traditional ones? 5) What is the general rule for stroke order? 6) What two parts make up 好 (hǎo)? Answers: 1) 'Chinese characters'. 2) the left part 女 (woman) gives the meaning; the right part 马 (mǎ) gives the sound. 3) 'woods' - two trees. 4) simplified on the mainland and in Singapore; traditional in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau. 5) generally top to bottom and left to right, with a fixed number of strokes. 6) 女 (nǚ, woman) and 子 (zǐ, child). Spotting the parts is the whole game.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking each character stands for a single letter or sound; a character is normally one whole syllable and one unit of meaning. Mistake: assuming the sound part of a character gives its exact modern pronunciation; it only hints at the sound, which may have drifted over the centuries. Mistake: treating simplified and traditional as different languages; they are two written standards for the same language, like two fonts of the same words. Mistake: drawing strokes in any order; order is fixed and matters for handwriting and for how the shape comes out. Exit ticket: (a) What is a radical, and what does it tell you? (b) Give the simplified and traditional forms of 'horse'. (c) What is the general direction of stroke order? Answers: a radical (部首) is the meaning part that also organizes dictionaries; 马 simplified and 馬 traditional; top to bottom and left to right.

questions.prompt: The syllable 'ma' said with a dipping tone, written mǎ, means...
questions.explanation: 妈 (mā) is 'mother', 麻 (má) is 'hemp', 马 (mǎ, third tone) is 'horse', and 骂 (mà) is 'to scold'.

questions.prompt: In Pinyin, the tone mark is written over...
options: the main vowel of the final
questions.explanation: The tone mark sits over the main vowel, as in hǎo and xué.

questions.prompt: In the character 妈 (mā), the 马 (mǎ) part mainly supplies the...
questions.explanation: 妈 pairs the woman radical 女 (meaning) with 马 (mǎ), which is there chiefly for the sound.

questions.prompt: Simplified characters (简体字) are used mainly in...
questions.explanation: Simplified forms are standard on the mainland and in Singapore; traditional forms are kept in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau.
三 (sān) is 'three'; 二 (èr) is 'two' and 十 (shí) is 'ten'.

questions.prompt: Mandarin has four main tones plus one more, which is called the...
questions.explanation: Beyond the four main tones there is a light, short neutral tone, written with no mark, as in the question word ma.

lessons.title: Building simple sentences
lessons.grammar_note: Mandarin word order is subject-verb-object; verbs and nouns never change their form, so grammar is shown by word order and small particles rather than by endings.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to build a basic Mandarin sentence in subject-verb-object order, turn a statement into a yes/no question with the particle 吗 (ma), make a sentence negative with 不 (bù), and use a measure word between a number and a noun. Warm-up: the English sentence 'I love you' has three words in the order subject, verb, object - what order do you think Mandarin uses? The good news for English speakers is that the basic order is the same. Even better, Mandarin words never change their form: verbs are not conjugated and nouns are not declined, so there are no endings to memorize. Grammar is carried instead by word order and by a small kit of particles, which makes the first sentences surprisingly quick to assemble once you know a little vocabulary.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The core order is subject, then verb, then object, exactly as in English. 我爱你 (Wǒ ài nǐ) means 'I love you': 我 (wǒ) 'I', 爱 (ài) 'love', 你 (nǐ) 'you'. To ask a yes/no question, you do not change the word order at all; you simply add the particle 吗 (ma) to the end. So 你好吗? (Nǐ hǎo ma?) means 'Are you well?' To make a sentence negative, put 不 (bù) 'not' before the verb: 我不喝茶 (Wǒ bù hē chá) means 'I do not drink tea'. One feature has no close English match: when you count nouns, you must slot a measure word between the number and the noun. The most common, general-purpose measure word is 个 (gè). So 'three people' is 三个人 (sān gè rén), literally 'three [measure] person'. Different nouns prefer different measure words, for example 本 (běn) for books: 一本书 (yì běn shū) is 'one book'.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Collect these sentence-building pieces, each with Pinyin and meaning. 我 (wǒ) 'I', 你 (nǐ) 'you', 他 (tā) 'he', 她 (tā) 'she' - note 他 and 她 sound identical and differ only in the written character. 是 (shì) is 'to be': 我是学生 (Wǒ shì xuéshēng) means 'I am a student'. 有 (yǒu) is 'to have': 我有一本书 (Wǒ yǒu yì běn shū) means 'I have one book', with the measure word 本 (běn). The possessive particle 的 (de) works like English apostrophe-s: 我的书 (wǒ de shū) is 'my book'. Questions and negatives in action: 你是学生吗? (Nǐ shì xuéshēng ma?) means 'Are you a student?', and the negative answer 我不是学生 (Wǒ bú shì xuéshēng) means 'I am not a student'. With measure words: 两个人 (liǎng gè rén) is 'two people' - note that 'two' before a measure word is 两 (liǎng), not 二 (èr).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Build or translate, then check. 1) Put 我 (wǒ), 爱 (ài), and 你 (nǐ) in order to say 'I love you'. 2) Turn 你好 (nǐ hǎo) into the question 'Are you well?' 3) Make 我喝茶 (Wǒ hē chá, I drink tea) negative. 4) Say 'three people' using 三 (sān), the measure word 个 (gè), and 人 (rén). 5) How do you say 'my book' using 的 (de)? 6) Which word means 'two' before a measure word? Answers: 1) 我爱你 (Wǒ ài nǐ). 2) 你好吗? (Nǐ hǎo ma?). 3) 我不喝茶 (Wǒ bù hē chá), putting 不 before the verb. 4) 三个人 (sān gè rén). 5) 我的书 (wǒ de shū). 6) 两 (liǎng), as in 两个人 (liǎng gè rén). Once the order and the particles click, you can mix and match words freely.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trying to conjugate verbs or add noun endings; Mandarin words keep one form, and grammar comes from order and particles. Mistake: reordering the sentence to ask a question; you keep the statement as it is and simply add 吗 (ma) at the end. Mistake: putting a number straight before a noun without a measure word; you need the measure word, as in 三个人 (sān gè rén), not 三人. Mistake: using 二 (èr) before a measure word, where the correct word is 两 (liǎng). Exit ticket: (a) What is the basic word order? (b) Which particle turns a statement into a yes/no question? (c) What must sit between a number and a noun? Answers: subject-verb-object; the particle 吗 (ma); a measure word, such as 个 (gè).

items.example: 你好！(Nǐ hǎo! - Hello!) Literally 'you good'.
谢谢你。(Xièxie nǐ. - Thank you.) The reply is 不客气 (bú kèqi - you're welcome).
我是学生。(Wǒ shì xuéshēng. - I am a student.)
你好吗？(Nǐ hǎo ma? - How are you?)
他是老师。(Tā shì lǎoshī. - He is a teacher.)

items.translation: jiào - to be called, to be named
items.example: 我叫李明。(Wǒ jiào Lǐ Míng. - My name is Li Ming.)
我不是老师。(Wǒ bú shì lǎoshī. - I am not a teacher.)

lessons.title: The culture and value of Mandarin
lessons.grammar_note: Learning Mandarin opens a very large world of speakers, media, and history; the writing system alone connects you to thousands of years of continuous written culture.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain several practical and cultural reasons for learning Mandarin, describe what makes the written language a cultural treasure in its own right, and set yourself a few realistic next steps. Warm-up: think back over this course - which single fact about Mandarin surprised you most, and why? This final lesson steps back from the mechanics of tones and characters to look at the bigger picture: what a speaker of Mandarin gains access to, and why so many people around the world choose to study it. Seeing the payoff clearly is not idle motivation; it helps you decide where to point your practice next, whether toward travel, reading, business, or simply the pleasure of understanding one of the world's great written traditions from the inside.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The most obvious reason to learn Mandarin is reach: with around a billion first-language speakers and many more who use it as a second language, it opens conversations across China, Taiwan, Singapore, and large communities worldwide. It is one of the official working languages of the United Nations. China is a major force in global trade, science, and manufacturing, so Mandarin is increasingly useful in business and research. Beyond the practical, the language carries a continuous written tradition thousands of years long: because the characters record meaning rather than only sound, a reader today can approach classical poetry, philosophy, and history in a script directly descended from the ancient forms. The culture is rich with features a learner comes to love - the four-character idioms called 成语 (chéngyǔ) that pack a whole story into four syllables, the art of brush calligraphy (书法, shūfǎ), and festivals, food, and film that reward even a little language knowledge with a great deal more understanding.

sections.heading: Key words & examples
sections.text: Here are words that open the cultural door, each with Pinyin and meaning. 文化 (wénhuà) means 'culture'. 历史 (lìshǐ) means 'history'. 成语 (chéngyǔ) are the four-character idioms, for example 马马虎虎 (mǎmǎhūhū), literally 'horse horse tiger tiger', used to mean 'so-so' or 'careless'. 书法 (shūfǎ) is 'calligraphy', long prized as a fine art. 朋友 (péngyou) means 'friend', and making friends is one of the great rewards of the language: 我们是朋友 (Wǒmen shì péngyou) means 'We are friends'. A gentle, famous saying captures the spirit of starting out: the proverb that a journey of a thousand 里 (lǐ, a traditional unit of distance) begins with a single step. You have already taken several steps - you can greet someone, count, read Pinyin, and recognize how a character is built, all of which were strangers to you at the start.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each, then check. 1) Give two practical reasons to learn Mandarin. 2) Why can a modern reader approach very old Chinese texts in a familiar script? 3) What is a 成语 (chéngyǔ)? 4) What does 书法 (shūfǎ) mean? 5) What does the idiom 马马虎虎 (mǎmǎhūhū) mean? 6) Name one skill you gained in this course. Answers: 1) for example, the huge number of speakers and Mandarin's role in global business and research (travel and study also count). 2) because characters record meaning rather than only sound, so the script has stayed recognizable across the centuries. 3) a four-character idiom that compresses a whole idea or story. 4) 'calligraphy', the art of beautiful writing. 5) 'so-so' or 'careless', literally 'horse horse tiger tiger'. 6) answers will vary - greeting someone, counting, or reading Pinyin all count.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing Mandarin is useful only inside China; it serves large communities in Taiwan, Singapore, and across the world, and it is a working language of the United Nations. Mistake: thinking the characters are merely a hard spelling system rather than a cultural achievement that links readers to a very long written past. Mistake: expecting to master tones and characters quickly; steady daily practice beats occasional long sessions, and small gains compound. Mistake: stopping here - the best next step is to keep saying words aloud and reading Pinyin every day. Exit ticket: (a) Name one global role of the Mandarin language. (b) What are 成语 (chéngyǔ)? (c) What is the best habit for keeping your new Mandarin alive? Answers: it is a working language of the United Nations (large speaker numbers and business use also count); four-character idioms; short, regular daily practice.
